subject: Banking
title: Market Making: The Hidden Spread
description: A 60-second lesson on Market Making: The Hidden Spread.

hook.text: Banks quote buy and sell prices for securities. They buy at $99.95 and sell at $100.05. That $0.10 spread is profit.

buildup.text: Market makers provide liquidity. They stand ready to buy or sell at any time, keeping markets functional.

discovery.text: On billions of daily trades, the spread adds up to enormous revenue.

twist.text: Electronic trading has compressed spreads. What was $0.10 is now $0.01. Banks make up for it with massive volume.

climax.text: Market making earns a tiny amount per trade on a massive number of trades. Scale is what makes it profitable.

punchline.text: Pennies per trade, billions in total. Market making profits from volume.

quiz.question: How do market makers profit?
options: By the bid-ask spread on each trade

details.summary: Banks make billions as market makers by standing ready to buy and sell securities, profiting from the bid-ask spread on every transaction. This invisible margin is embedded in every bond, stock, and derivative trade that flows through bank trading desks.
details.whyItMatters: Market making is one of banking's most profitable but least understood activities. The spread on trillions in daily trading volume generates enormous revenue while providing essential liquidity to financial markets.
takeaways: Banks quote both buy and sell prices, profiting from the difference
Market making provides essential liquidity for financial markets to function
The largest banks earn billions annually from market-making operations

faq.question: How do market makers profit from the spread?
faq.answer: A market maker might offer to buy a bond at $99.90 and sell at $100.10. The $0.20 difference is pure profit on each round trip. Across millions of trades and trillions in volume, these small spreads generate billions in annual revenue.

faq.question: Is market making risky for banks?
faq.answer: Market makers hold inventory of securities that can lose value if markets move against them. During volatile periods, spreads widen but inventory risk increases. Banks manage this through hedging and position limits, but losses can be significant during crises.
